questions.q: Explain EA = S + B + T using a real example.
questions.m: Strategy says where the organization is going, business says what it delivers, and technology supports delivery. A bank aiming to grow online (strategy) offers mobile accounts (business) using a mobile app and cloud services (technology).

questions.q: Which is one of the six elements of EA analysis and design?
questions.e: The six are framework, components, current, future, management plan and threads.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a level, a line of business and a thread.
questions.m: A level is a horizontal layer such as Data & Information. A line of business is a vertical functional area such as Finance. A thread such as security runs through every level.

questions.q: What three things drive the future architecture?
questions.m: New strategic directions and goals, changing business priorities, and emerging technologies.

questions.q: Student enrolment records defined independently of any system belong to:
questions.e: Level 3 is defined independent of where it is stored.

questions.e: It uses historical Data & Information to forecast demand on Levels 4 and 5.

questions.q: Process mining mainly helps with:
Trace a goal of "24-hour customer support" through all five EA levels.
questions.m: L1: the 24-hour support goal. L2: a chat support service. L3: customer tickets and history. L4: a chatbot and ticketing application. L5: cloud hosting and network capacity.

questions.q: Compare top-down and bottom-up planning in EA.
questions.m: Top-down starts with strategy, which creates requirements for each lower level and is the normal direction. Bottom-up starts with a technology that makes new services or goals possible.

questions.q: Give two ways AI changes EA documentation.
questions.m: AI can find patterns across levels to support strategic decisions, and it can forecast demand on systems through predictive analytics. Documentation becomes an active tool rather than a static file.

Name the four parts of the EA Management Plan and the question each answers.
questions.m: Program Management: how is it run? Current Summary: what exists today? Future Summary: where are we headed? Glossary and References: what do our terms mean?

questions.q: Explain why EA is a program rather than a project.
questions.m: A project ends when its deliverable is done, while the enterprise keeps changing. The architecture must be managed and updated continuously, with ongoing governance, staffing and budget.

questions.q: Write a one-line example for each part of a plan for a hospital.
questions.m: Program: a Chief Architect reports to the CIO. Current: three separate patient-record systems. Future: one unified record system in 2 years. Glossary: defines "patient record" and cites privacy regulations.

Describe the structure of the EA repository.
questions.m: It's a grid of six columns (the five levels plus Security Solutions) and three views: high level, mid level and detailed.

questions.q: Why does the repository add Security Solutions when security is already a thread?
questions.m: Security runs through all levels as a thread, but it also needs dedicated documentation for audiences such as auditors and compliance officers.

questions.q: State two reasons the repository matters.
questions.m: It gives every stakeholder one source of truth at the right level of detail, and it keeps the EA Management Plan's documents current and consistent.

questions.q: List the four EA risks and give one mitigation for each.
questions.m: Financial: solidify budgets. Loss of key personnel: trained back-ups. Lack of acceptance: strengthen executive support. Schedule delays: a detailed methodology and program management skills.

questions.q: Describe the pattern of EA program costs.
questions.m: The cost should be viewed across the full lifecycle. Setup costs more than maintenance, and labour is by far the largest cost.

Apply the Leavitt Diamond to a university's new online exam system.
questions.m: Technology changes with the new system. People need training. Tasks change, since exams are delivered and graded online. Structure may change with a new team to support it. A change in one affects the others.

questions.q: Describe the three levels of the Parsons/Thompson Model.
questions.m: The Institutional level relates to society and establishes legitimacy. The Managerial level mediates with the task environment and coordinates. The Technical level performs the core work.

questions.m: Life cycle: Identify, Analyze, Design, Execute, Measure. Four phases: Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, Recovery.

questions.q: Compare hot and cold sites.
questions.m: A hot site is fully equipped so business can resume immediately, at high cost. A cold site has no computer equipment, so it's cheaper but much slower.

questions.q: Explain the disaster recovery cost curve.
questions.m: As time passes after a disaster, the cost of unavailability rises while the cost to recover falls. The optimal disaster recovery plan is at the crossing point.

questions.q: Define the three elements of strategy, with an example of each.
questions.m: Goals are primary long-term objectives, such as compliance. Initiatives are the programs that enable them, such as an API platform. Measures show when a goal is met, such as integrations live in 12 months.

questions.q: Why shouldn't technology drive business planning?
questions.m: Technology exists to support business requirements. If it drives planning, organizations invest in duplicative or non-strategic technologies, which resource-constrained enterprises can't afford.

questions.q: Trace "reduce patient waiting time" through strategy, business and technology.
questions.m: Strategy: goal is shorter waits, initiative is online booking, measure is average wait under 20 minutes. Business: a documented online booking service. Technology: a booking application that supports it.

Moving from IaaS to SaaS, the customer gets:
Compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, stating who controls what and giving an example.
questions.m: IaaS: you control the OS and apps, and the provider runs hardware, such as Amazon EC2. PaaS: you control your deployed app, and the provider runs the platform, such as Google App Engine. SaaS: you control only settings and the provider does everything else, such as Gmail.

questions.q: Explain how SOA improves on siloed systems.
questions.m: Siloed systems duplicate logic and are brittle. SOA exposes business tasks as reusable services with defined interfaces, making applications interoperable and easier to change.

questions.q: Describe how virtualization saves money, with an example.
questions.m: One powerful physical server can run several virtual machines instead of buying a separate server for each system. For example, a university can run accounting, marketing and the student portal on one machine.

Describe the structure of the Zachman Framework.
questions.m: It's a 6×6 matrix of 36 cells. Rows are perspectives from executive to enterprise, and columns are the six questions: what, how, where, who, when and why.

questions.q: For each of the four frameworks, state when you'd use it.
questions.m: Zachman to check that nothing is undocumented. TOGAF for a repeatable process. EA3 Cube for a structured repository and management plan. DoDAF for defense or government interoperability.

questions.q: Why can Zachman be combined with TOGAF?
questions.m: Zachman classifies what to document and TOGAF gives the process for how to build it, so they complement rather than compete with each other.

questions.m: Preliminary, A Vision, B Business, C Information Systems, D Technology, E Opportunities and Solutions, F Migration Planning, G Implementation Governance and H Change Management, with Requirements Management at the centre.

questions.q: Distinguish deliverable, artifact and building block.
questions.m: A deliverable is a contractually specified work product signed off by stakeholders. An artifact is a catalog, diagram or matrix that forms part of a deliverable. A building block is a potentially reusable component.

questions.q: What three things do Phases B, C and D each do?
questions.m: Each develops the baseline architecture, develops the target architecture, and identifies the gaps between them.

questions.q: Locate a hospital's patient-records database in the cube.
questions.m: Level: Systems & Applications, or Data & Information for the records themselves. Segment: Clinical Services. Artifact: an application inventory entry or a data model.

questions.q: Name the three pitfalls and how to avoid them.
questions.m: Don't treat levels as steps, as they're simultaneous views. Don't ignore the security, standards and skills threads. And don't assume that one cube is enough for a large enterprise.

questions.q: Explain the difference between levels and segments.
questions.m: Levels are horizontal slices that say what kind of thing it is. Segments are vertical slices that say which part of the business it belongs to.

Which is one of the reasons for AI in EA now?
questions.e: Documentation volume, mature tools and faster change.

questions.q: Suggestions that repeat gaps in old documents reflect:
Under the course policy, AI-assisted work must be:
Name the three AI capabilities in EA with one example each.
questions.m: AI-assisted modeling drafts Current Architecture from existing documents. AI-supported governance flags drift from standards. Smart repositories use semantic search to find related work across segments.

questions.q: State the three limitations of AI in EA.
questions.m: Hallucinated documentation, governance blind spots where a standard was never documented, and training data bias that carries forward old gaps.

questions.q: Why must an architect review AI drafts?
questions.m: AI can produce plausible but incorrect entries, so a person must verify them against source systems before they become official. AI doesn't replace architectural judgment.
